title: Training science
note: The body adapts to the specific demands placed on it, so training must match the sport and rise gradually: progressive overload. Planned variation and recovery let adaptation happen. Combat sports draw on all three energy systems, and a good warm-up raises temperature, activates and mobilizes, then sharpens with sport-like movement.

read.title: Overload, specificity, and recovery
text: Strength coaches build programs on a few principles. Specificity says the body adapts to the particular demands placed on it, so a fighter who must work hard for three-minute rounds should condition with similar efforts and rests, not only long slow runs. Progressive overload says those demands must rise over time, by adding intensity, frequency, or difficulty, at a pace the athlete can absorb.

Adaptation happens during recovery, not during the workout itself. Hard training creates fatigue; with rest, sleep, and food the body rebuilds and can rise above its earlier level, an effect called supercompensation. Periodization organizes this rhythm into phases, from week-long microcycles to blocks of several weeks and whole seasons, often with a lighter deload week before the next push. Planned variation keeps progress from stalling.

Combat sports draw on every energy system: the phosphagen system for explosive bursts, glycolysis for hard scrambles lasting up to a couple of minutes, and the aerobic system for recovering between exchanges. A good warm-up follows the RAMP pattern: raise temperature, activate and mobilize, then potentiate with sharp, sport-like movement.
